docs.title: vexy-glob
docs.text:
vexy-glob finds files and searches their contents from Python. The work happens in a Rust extension module built on the ignore crate (the directory walker behind fd) and the grep-searcher crate (the search engine behind ripgrep). Python receives the matching paths as they are found, through an iterator, so the first results arrive before the walk finishes.

The import name is vexy_glob. The PyPI package name is vexy-glob. The command-line tool is vg.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
You give it a glob pattern, a starting directory and optional filters. It walks the directory tree on several threads, skips what .gitignore and hidden-file rules exclude, applies your filters, and yields each path that passes.

import vexy_glob

for path in vexy_glob.find("*.py", root="src"):
    print(path)

With a project that contains src/a.py and src/sub/b.py, this prints:

src/a.py
src/sub/b.py

The order can differ from run to run, because several threads walk the tree at once. Pass sort="path" when you need a stable order.

Add a regular expression with content= (or call search()) and the tool reads each matching file and yields one dictionary per matching line:

for hit in vexy_glob.search("TODO", "*.py", root="src"):
    print(f"{hit['path']}:{hit['line_number']}:{hit['line_text'].rstrip()}")

src/sub/b.py:1:TODO x

docs.title: Main features
docs.text:
• Streaming results. find() returns an iterator by default. Pass as_list=True to get a list.
  • Ignore rules. .gitignore, .ignore, .git/info/exclude and a root .fdignore file are honoured unless you pass ignore_git=True.
  • Filters. File type, extension, exclude patterns, size, modification time, access time, creation time and depth.
  • Smart case. A pattern without uppercase letters matches case-insensitively. A pattern with an uppercase letter matches case-sensitively.
  • Content search. Regular expressions in Rust regex syntax, run only on files that pass the path filters.
  • glob replacements. vexy_glob.glob() and vexy_glob.iglob() accept the common arguments of glob.glob() and glob.iglob().
  • CLI. vg find and vg search expose the same engine in the terminal.

docs.title: Python API
docs.text:
Everything public is exported from the vexy_glob package:

from vexy_glob import (
    find, glob, iglob, search,
    VexyGlobError, PatternError, SearchError, TraversalNotSupportedError,
)

vexy_glob.__version__ holds the installed package version, read from the package metadata.

docs.title: find()
docs.text:
find(
    pattern: str = "*",
    root: str | Path = ".",
    *,
    content: str | None = None,
    file_type: str | None = None,
    extension: str | list[str] | None = None,
    exclude: str | list[str] | None = None,
    max_depth: int | None = None,
    min_depth: int = 0,
    min_size: int | None = None,
    max_size: int | None = None,
    mtime_after: float | int | str | datetime | None = None,
    mtime_before: float | int | str | datetime | None = None,
    atime_after: float | int | str | datetime | None = None,
    atime_before: float | int | str | datetime | None = None,
    ctime_after: float | int | str | datetime | None = None,
    ctime_before: float | int | str | datetime | None = None,
    hidden: bool = False,
    ignore_git: bool = False,
    custom_ignore_files: str | list[str] | None = None,
    case_sensitive: bool | None = None,
    follow_symlinks: bool = False,
    same_file_system: bool = False,
    sort: "name" | "path" | "size" | "mtime" | None = None,
    threads: int | None = None,
    as_path: bool = False,
    as_list: bool = False,
)

Walks root, applies the filters and returns the matching paths. With content, returns search results instead (see Content search).

Everything after root is keyword-only.

Parameter Default Meaning pattern "*" Glob pattern. Without / it matches at any depth. See Patterns and case. root "." Directory to walk. Returned paths start with it. content None Regex to search for inside matching files. file_type None "f", "d" or "l". extension None Extension or list of extensions, without the dot. exclude None Glob pattern or list of patterns to drop. max_depth None Deepest level to visit; the root is level 0. min_depth 0 Accepted but not applied in the current release. min_size, max_size None Inclusive size limits in bytes, applied to regular files. mtime_after, mtime_before None Modification-time limits. atime_after, atime_before None Access-time limits. ctime_after, ctime_before None Creation-time limits. hidden False Include entries whose name starts with a dot. ignore_git False Stop honouring .gitignore, .ignore, .git/info/exclude and .fdignore. custom_ignore_files None Extra ignore files in gitignore syntax. case_sensitive None None is smart case; True or False forces a mode for glob and regex. follow_symlinks False Descend into linked directories. same_file_system False Do not cross mount points. sort None Sort key; forces a list result. Ignored when content is set. threads None Walker threads; None or 0 means one per logical CPU. as_path False Return pathlib.Path objects instead of strings. as_list False Return a list instead of an iterator.

Time values accept Unix timestamps, datetime objects, ISO date strings and relative strings such as "-2h". See Filters.

Returns

Call Return value no content, no sort, as_list=False Iterator of str (or Path) no content, as_list=True or sort set list of str (or Path) content set, as_list=False Iterator of result dictionaries content set, as_list=True list of result dictionaries

Raises

  • ImportError if the compiled extension is missing (for example in a source checkout before maturin develop).
  • PatternError for a glob or exclude pattern that cannot be parsed.
  • ValueError for a time string in an unknown format, TypeError for a time value of another type.
  • VexyGlobError for other errors reported by the Rust core, such as an invalid regex or an unknown sort value.

A root that does not exist does not raise. The walker reports Error during traversal: ... No such file or directory on standard error (iterator mode) and the result is empty.

docs.title: glob()
docs.text:
glob(
    pattern: str,
    *,
    recursive: bool = False,
    root_dir: str | Path | None = None,
    include_hidden: bool = False,
) -> list[str]

Accepts the common keyword arguments of glob.glob() and returns a list of strings. It calls find(pattern, root=root_dir or ".", hidden=include_hidden, as_list=True).

  • recursive=True puts **/ in front of the pattern if it contains no **.
  • root_dir sets the directory to search. Returned paths start with it.

Because a pattern without / already matches at any depth (see Patterns and case), glob("*.py") also returns files in subdirectories, unlike glob.glob("*.py"). Paths start with ./ when root_dir is not given. .gitignore rules apply.

docs.title: iglob()
docs.text:
iglob(
    pattern: str,
    *,
    recursive: bool = False,
    root_dir: str | Path | None = None,
    include_hidden: bool = False,
) -> Iterator[str]

Same as glob(), but returns an iterator.

docs.title: search()
docs.text:
search(
    content_regex: str,
    pattern: str = "*",
    root: str | Path = ".",
    **kwargs,
)

Searches file contents. Equivalent to find(pattern=pattern, root=root, content=content_regex, **kwargs), after removing sort from kwargs. Returns an iterator of result dictionaries, or a list with as_list=True.

Each result dictionary has the keys path, line_number, line_text and matches. See Content search.

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text:
Exception
└── VexyGlobError
    ├── PatternError          (also a ValueError)
    ├── SearchError           (also an IOError / OSError)
    └── TraversalNotSupportedError  (also a NotImplementedError)
Exception When VexyGlobError Base class. Also raised for Rust-side errors that fit no subclass. PatternError A glob or exclude pattern is invalid. The pattern attribute holds the main pattern argument, even when the bad pattern was in exclude; the message names the bad one. SearchError An error message from the Rust core mentions permissions or I/O. TraversalNotSupportedError Defined for API compatibility; the current code does not raise it.

Catch VexyGlobError to handle all of them in one place:

try:
    files = vexy_glob.find(user_pattern, as_list=True)
except vexy_glob.PatternError as e:
    print(f"Bad pattern {e.pattern!r}")
except vexy_glob.VexyGlobError as e:
    print(f"Search failed: {e}")

docs.title: The extension module
docs.text: The compiled module is vexy_glob._vexy_glob. It exposes lower-level find() and search() functions that the Python layer calls. They take a list of root paths, Unix timestamps as floats and pre-computed case flags. Treat them as internal: their signatures can change between releases.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
vexy-glob has two layers: a thin Python package that normalises arguments, and a Rust extension module that walks the file system, filters entries and searches file contents.

vexy_glob/__init__.py      Python API: find, glob, iglob, search, exceptions
vexy_glob/__main__.py      CLI (Fire): vg find, vg search
src/lib.rs                 PyO3 module vexy_glob._vexy_glob: walker, filters, search
src/pattern_cache.rs       Compiled glob cache (LRU, 1000 entries)
src/global_init.rs         One-time initialisation when the module is imported
src/zero_copy_path.rs      Path helpers prepared for later use (not called yet)
src/simd_string.rs         String helpers prepared for later use (not called yet)

docs.title: Python layer
docs.text:
vexy_glob.find() does no file-system work itself. It:

  1. Converts a Path root to str.
  2. Works out the case mode. With case_sensitive=None, the glob is case-sensitive if it contains an uppercase letter, and the content regex is checked the same way on its own.
  3. Turns single strings for extension, exclude and custom_ignore_files into one-element lists.
  4. Converts every time argument to a Unix timestamp (float). Relative values such as "-2h" are resolved against time.time() at this point.
  5. Calls _vexy_glob.find() or, when content is set, _vexy_glob.search().
  6. Maps errors from the Rust side to PatternError, SearchError or VexyGlobError by looking at the error message.

glob(), iglob() and search() are small wrappers around find().

docs.title: Walking
docs.text:
The core builds an ignore::WalkBuilder for the root and configures it from the arguments:

Builder setting Set from hidden(!hidden) hidden ignore, git_ignore, git_exclude not ignore_git git_global(true) always on follow_links follow_symlinks same_file_system same_file_system max_depth max_depth threads threads, or the CPU count when 0 add_ignore(path) each existing file in custom_ignore_files, and <root>/.fdignore unless ignore_git

It then starts the parallel walker (build_parallel()) on a separate thread and returns to Python.

docs.title: Filtering
docs.text:
Each walker thread runs every entry through one function, should_include_entry(), which checks in this order: glob pattern, exclude patterns, file type, extension, size, modification time, access time and creation time. The first failed check rejects the entry. Size and time checks read the entry's metadata only when such a filter is set.

Glob patterns are compiled once and kept in a process-wide cache keyed by pattern and case mode. A pattern with no wildcard characters skips globset and is compared as a plain string.

docs.title: Streaming results to Python
docs.text:
Accepted paths go into a bounded crossbeam-channel channel. Its capacity depends on the job:

Job Channel capacity Content search 500 Path search with sort 10,000 Path search, threads not set 1,000 Path search, threads=n 1,000 × n, at most 8,000

When Python asks for an iterator, the core wraps the receiving end of the channel in a VexyGlobIterator object. Each next() call takes one result from the channel and converts it to a str, a pathlib.Path or, for content search, a dict. If Python reads slower than the walker produces, the channel fills up and the walker threads wait, so memory use stays bounded.

When Python asks for a list (as_list=True or sort), the core releases the GIL, drains the channel while the walker runs, then joins the walker thread, sorts if requested, and builds a Python list. Releases up to 1.0.9 joined the walker first and could hang on large result sets; see Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Content search
docs.text: For search(), entries that pass should_include_entry() and are regular files are opened and scanned with a grep_searcher::Searcher and a grep_regex::RegexMatcher. A custom sink collects one record per matching line (path, line number, line text) and sends the records for a file to the channel after the file is finished.

docs.title: Errors during the walk
docs.text: Walker errors (unreadable directories, a missing root) and file-open errors travel through the same channel as error records. The iterator prints them to standard error with the prefix Error during traversal: and moves on. The list path discards them.

docs.title: Build and packaging
docs.text:
The project is a maturin "mixed" layout (python-source = "." in pyproject.toml): maturin compiles the crate in src/ into vexy_glob/_vexy_glob.*.so (or .pyd on Windows) and packages it together with the Python files in vexy_glob/. PyO3 is built with the abi3-py38 feature, so one wheel per platform works on CPython 3.8 and newer.

The release profile in Cargo.toml uses opt-level = 3, LTO, one codegen unit, panic = "abort" and stripped symbols.

The package version is the version in Cargo.toml; pyproject.toml declares it as dynamic. See Contributing for how a release keeps the git tag and Cargo.toml in step.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text: Installing the package adds a vg command with two subcommands, find and search. The CLI is built with Python Fire (vexy_glob/__main__.py), and each subcommand calls the matching Python function.

docs.title: vg find
docs.text:
Prints one path per line.

vg find [PATTERN] [options]

PATTERN defaults to *. Quote it so the shell does not expand it.

Option Short Value Python argument --root -r Directory to start in (default .) root --min-size Size string, see below min_size --max-size Size string, see below max_size --mtime-after Time string, e.g. -2d, 2025-01-01 mtime_after --mtime-before Time string mtime_before --no-gitignore -n Flag ignore_git=True --hidden -h Flag hidden=True --case-sensitive -c Flag, or False case_sensitive --type -t f, d or l file_type --extension -e Extension without the dot extension --depth -d Integer max_depth

Fire accepts both --min-size and --min_size. Note that -h means --hidden; to see help, run vg find --help.

Examples:

# Python files anywhere below the current directory
vg find "*.py"

# Markdown files of at least 10 KiB
vg find "*.md" --min-size 10k

# Log files changed in the last two days
vg find "*.log" --mtime-after -2d

# Directories, one level deep
vg find "*" --type d --depth 1

# Search another directory and include hidden files
vg find "*.toml" --root ~/projects --hidden

The CLI exposes a subset of the API. Filters such as exclude, atime_*, ctime_*, follow_symlinks and sort are available from Python only.

docs.title: vg search
docs.text:
Prints one line per match in the form path:line_number:line_text.

vg search PATTERN CONTENT_PATTERN [options]
  • PATTERN is the glob for the files to search.
  • CONTENT_PATTERN is the regular expression to look for.

vg search accepts every option of vg find plus:

Option Value Effect --no-color Flag Plain text. Without it, the path is printed in magenta and the line number in green.

Examples:

vg search "*.py" "import asyncio"
vg search "*.rs" "fn\s+main" --root src
vg search "*.md" "TODO" --no-color | cut -d: -f1 | sort -u

./src/sub/b.py:1:TODO x

The trailing line ending of each match is removed before printing.

docs.title: Size strings
docs.text:
--min-size and --max-size take a number followed by an optional unit:

Unit Multiplier none or b 1 k 1,024 M 1,048,576 G 1,073,741,824 T 1,099,511,627,776

Units are case-insensitive and may be followed by b or B (10kb, 1MB). Decimals are allowed (1.5M).

Give the size with a unit. Fire turns a bare number such as 500 into an integer, and the size parser then fails with Error: 'int' object has no attribute 'strip'. Write 500b instead.

docs.title: Output and exit codes
docs.text:
• Results are written to standard output as they are found.
  • Errors are printed to standard output as Error: <message>, and the command exits with status 1.
  • Ctrl+C exits with status 130.
  • A closed pipe (for example vg find "*" | head -1) stops the command without an error message. In the current release the exit status is then 1, which matters only if your shell uses set -o pipefail.

docs.title: Running without the entry point
docs.text:
python -m vexy_glob runs the same CLI:

python -m vexy_glob find "*.py"

docs.title: Content search
docs.text: Content search reads the files that pass the path filters and reports every line that matches a regular expression. It uses the grep-searcher and grep-regex crates from ripgrep.

docs.title: Two ways to call it
docs.text:
search() takes the regex first:

vexy_glob.search(content_regex, pattern="*", root=".", **kwargs)

find() with content= does the same thing:

vexy_glob.find(pattern, root=".", content=content_regex, ...)

search() removes a sort argument if you pass one and then calls find(). All other keyword arguments (filters, hidden, as_list and so on) work the same way as for find().

docs.title: What happens to one file
docs.text:
Take src/sub/b.py containing the single line TODO x, and the call search("TODO", "*.py", root="src"):

  1. The walker reaches src/sub/b.py.
  2. The path filters run: *.py matches, there are no other filters.
  3. The entry is a regular file, so the searcher opens it. (Directories and links never reach the searcher.)
  4. The searcher runs the regex over the file line by line and records one result for each matching line.
  5. When the file is done, its results are sent to Python in order.

The result is:

{'path': 'src/sub/b.py', 'line_number': 1, 'line_text': 'TODO x\n', 'matches': ['TODO x']}

Results from one file arrive in line order. Results from different files can interleave, because files are searched on several threads.

docs.title: The result dictionary
Regex syntax
docs.text:
The regex is compiled by the Rust regex engine through grep-regex. Its syntax is close to Python's re, with these differences that matter in practice:

  • No look-around ((?=...), (?!...), (?<=...), (?<!...)) and no backreferences. Patterns that use them raise an error.
  • Matching is line-oriented: each line is searched on its own, so a regex cannot match across a line break.
  • \b, \d, \w, \s, character classes, alternation and repetition work as expected. Write patterns as raw strings in Python (r"fn\s+\w+").

Case follows smart case (see Patterns and case): a regex without uppercase letters is case-insensitive. case_sensitive=True or False overrides it for both the glob and the regex.

An invalid regex raises VexyGlobError:

>>> vexy_glob.search("(", "*.py", as_list=True)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
vexy_glob.VexyGlobError: Invalid content regex: regex parse error:
    (?:()
    ^
error: unclosed group

docs.title: Streaming versus lists
docs.text:
Like find(), search() returns an iterator unless you pass as_list=True. The iterator lets you stop early:

first = next(iter(vexy_glob.search("def main", "*.py")), None)

docs.title: Narrowing the search
docs.text:
Path filters run before any file is opened, so they reduce the amount of data read from disk. Useful combinations:

# Only Python sources, skip tests, skip files over 1 MiB
vexy_glob.search(
    r"import\s+asyncio",
    "*.py",
    root="src",
    exclude="*test*",
    max_size=1024 * 1024,
)

# Only recently changed Markdown files
vexy_glob.search("FIXME", "*.md", mtime_after="-7d")

docs.title: Errors while searching
docs.text:
If a file cannot be opened or read, the error is reported and the search goes on:

  • With an iterator, the message is printed to standard error, prefixed with Error during traversal:, and iteration continues with the next result.
  • With as_list=True, such errors are dropped silently.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: The source lives at https://github.com/vexyart/vexy-glob. Bug reports and pull requests go to the GitHub issue tracker and pull request queue.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python 3.8 or newer (3.12 is used in the examples)
  • A Rust toolchain from https://rustup.rs/, with rustfmt and clippy
  • uv

docs.title: Set up a development build
docs.text:
1. Clone the repository and enter it:

    git clone https://github.com/vexyart/vexy-glob.git
cd vexy-glob

  2. Create and activate a virtual environment:

    uv venv --python 3.12
source .venv/bin/activate

  3. Install the build and test tools:

    uv pip install maturin pytest pytest-benchmark fire rich

  4. Compile the extension into the environment:

    maturin develop

    Repeat this step after every change to a .rs file. Python-only changes in vexy_glob/ take effect without rebuilding.

docs.title: Run the tests
docs.text:
Command What it runs python -m pytest tests/ -v Python test suite (tests/test_*.py) cargo test Rust unit tests in src/ cargo bench Criterion benchmarks in benches/

The tests/platform_tests/ directory holds platform-specific checks with their own runner, tests/platform_tests/run_platform_tests.py.

docs.title: Code style
docs.text:
Python:

uvx ruff check vexy_glob/ tests/
uvx ruff format vexy_glob/ tests/

pyproject.toml sets target-version = "py38" and a line length of 100. Keep the code importable on Python 3.8.

Rust:

cargo fmt
cargo clippy -- -D warnings

The CI workflow runs cargo fmt -- --check and cargo clippy -- -D warnings.

docs.title: Build the documentation
docs.text:
The documentation sources are the Markdown files in src_docs/md/, and the configuration is src_docs/mkdocs.yml. The site is built with ProperDocs and the MaterialX theme into docs/, which GitHub Pages serves at https://vexy.dev/vexy-glob/.

  1. Preview with live reload:

    src_docs/build.sh serve

    Open http://127.0.0.1:8000.

  2. Build the site in strict mode:

    src_docs/build.sh

    Any warning, such as a broken link between pages, stops the build.

You do not need to commit docs/ by hand. The Docs workflow (.github/workflows/docs.yml) rebuilds it on every push to main that changes src_docs/, and commits the result.

docs.title: Build the package
docs.text:
./build.sh package

This deletes dist/, runs uv build (source distribution plus one wheel for the current machine, built by maturin from the source distribution) and runs twine check on the results. ./build.sh with no argument builds the documentation as well; ./build.sh docs builds only the documentation.

docs.title: Why the version needs care
docs.text: maturin writes the version from Cargo.toml into every wheel and the source distribution. It does not read git tags. A tag v1.2.3 on a commit whose Cargo.toml says 1.2.2 would publish files labelled 1.2.2. Also, a local build produces a wheel for one platform only, so the published wheels must come from CI.

docs.title: The release procedure
docs.text:
Prerequisites: push access to vexyart/vexy-glob, uv on your PATH, and a working tree whose uncommitted changes you are ready to release, because the script commits all of them.

  1. Add a section for the new version to CHANGELOG.md, headed ## [X.Y.Z]. The GitHub release takes its notes from that section.

  2. Run the release script from the repository root:

    ./publish.sh

    The script:

    1. fetches tags from origin and stops if your branch is behind its upstream;
    2. finds the highest vX.Y.Z tag and adds 1 to the patch number, the same rule gitnextver uses (v1.0.10 becomes v1.0.11);
    3. stops if that tag already exists;
    4. writes the new version into Cargo.toml;
    5. runs ./build.sh package as a check that the package still builds;
    6. runs uvx gitnextver, which commits all pending changes with the tag name as the message, creates the tag and pushes the branch and the tags;
    7. checks that HEAD carries the tag it computed in step 2.

    Nothing is uploaded from your machine.

  3. Watch the Release workflow in the repository's Actions tab. On the tag push it:

    1. fails early if the tag does not equal the Cargo.toml version;
    2. builds wheels for Linux (x86_64, aarch64), macOS (x86_64, arm64) and Windows (x64), and the source distribution, with PyO3/maturin-action;
    3. uploads all files to PyPI with uv publish, skipping files that are already there;
    4. creates the GitHub release.

  4. Check the result on https://pypi.org/project/vexy-glob/.

The upload step needs PyPI credentials in the repository: either a PYPI_API_TOKEN secret, or a PyPI trusted publisher configured for the vexyart/vexy-glob repository and the release.yml workflow.

docs.title: If something goes wrong
docs.text:
• The script stops before gitnextver. Nothing was committed or pushed. Cargo.toml may already hold the new version; keep it or restore it with git checkout Cargo.toml.
  • The tag check in the workflow fails. The tag and Cargo.toml disagree. Nothing was uploaded. Delete the tag locally and on GitHub, fix Cargo.toml, and release again.
  • A wheel job fails. Nothing was uploaded, because the upload job waits for all build jobs. Fix the problem and re-run the failed jobs, or release a new patch version.

docs.title: Filters
docs.text: Every filter is a keyword argument of find(), and search() passes its extra keyword arguments on to find(). Filters combine with AND: an entry is returned only if it passes all of them. The walker applies them in the Rust core, so rejected entries never reach Python.

docs.title: File type
docs.text:
file_type keeps one kind of entry:

Value Keeps "f" Regular files "d" Directories "l" Symbolic links 
>>> vexy_glob.find("*", file_type="d", sort="path")
['.', './src', './src/sub']

Without file_type, results include files, directories and links. Any other value is ignored and no type filter is applied.

docs.title: Extension
docs.text:
extension takes one extension or a list, written without the leading dot:

vexy_glob.find("*", extension="py")
vexy_glob.find("*", extension=["py", "pyi"])

The comparison is exact and case-sensitive, and it uses the part after the last dot. Entries without an extension (including most directories) are dropped. extension=".py" matches nothing, because the stored extension is py.

docs.title: Exclude patterns
docs.text:
exclude takes one glob pattern or a list. An entry whose path matches any of them is dropped:

vexy_glob.find("*.py", exclude=["*_test.py", "**/build/**"])

Exclude patterns follow the same rules as the main pattern (see Patterns and case): a pattern without / gets a **/ prefix, and the case mode of the main pattern applies. Exclusion removes the matching entries from the results. It does not stop the walker from entering an excluded directory, so prefer .gitignore or a custom ignore file for large trees you never want to visit.

docs.title: Size
docs.text:
min_size and max_size are byte counts and both limits are inclusive. They apply only to regular files; directories and links pass through unchanged, so combine them with file_type="f" to get files only.

# Files from 1 KiB up to 10 MiB
vexy_glob.find("*", file_type="f", min_size=1024, max_size=10 * 1024 * 1024)

The command line accepts sizes such as 10k or 1M and converts them to bytes. The Python API takes integers only.

docs.title: Time
docs.text:
Six parameters filter by timestamp:

Parameter Timestamp used Keeps entries mtime_after last modification modified at or after the value mtime_before last modification modified at or before the value atime_after last access accessed at or after the value atime_before last access accessed at or before the value ctime_after creation time created at or after the value ctime_before creation time created at or before the value

ctime_* uses the file's creation (birth) time as reported by Rust's Metadata::created(). If a timestamp cannot be read (some Linux file systems do not record creation time), the entry is kept: the time filter does not remove it. Access times depend on the mount options of the file system (for example noatime or relatime on Linux).

Each value can be:

Form Example Meaning int or float 1735689600 Unix timestamp in seconds datetime datetime(2025, 1, 1) Converted with .timestamp() ISO date "2025-01-01" Midnight at the start of that day, local time ISO date and time "2025-01-01T12:30:00" That moment; a trailing Z means UTC Relative "-30s", "-15m", "-2h", "-7d" That long before now

Relative values start with - and end with s, m, h or d. A string that fits none of these forms raises ValueError.

from datetime import datetime

# Modified in the last two hours
vexy_glob.find("*.log", mtime_after="-2h")

# Modified during January 2025
vexy_glob.find("*", mtime_after="2025-01-01", mtime_before="2025-02-01")

# Not accessed since a fixed date
vexy_glob.find("*", file_type="f", atime_before=datetime(2024, 6, 1))

docs.title: Depth
docs.text:
max_depth limits how far the walker descends. The root is depth 0, its direct children are depth 1, and so on:

>>> vexy_glob.find("*", max_depth=0, as_list=True)
['.']
>>> vexy_glob.find("*.py", max_depth=2, as_list=True)
['./src/a.py']

./src/a.py is at depth 2 and ./src/sub/b.py at depth 3, so only the first is returned.

find() also accepts a min_depth argument, but the current release does not pass it to the Rust core, so it has no effect.

docs.title: Hidden files
docs.text: Entries whose name starts with a dot are skipped by default, together with everything below a hidden directory. Pass hidden=True to include them.

docs.title: Ignore files
docs.text:
By default the walker honours, like fd and ripgrep:

  • .gitignore files, the repository's .git/info/exclude and your global Git ignore file. The ignore crate applies Git rules only inside a Git repository.
  • .ignore files.
  • A .fdignore file in the root directory, if one exists.

Pass ignore_git=True to turn off the .gitignore, .ignore, .git/info/exclude and .fdignore handling. The global Git ignore file is still read.

custom_ignore_files adds more ignore files in gitignore syntax. Give one path or a list. Paths are checked relative to the current working directory, and files that do not exist are skipped without an error:

vexy_glob.find("*", custom_ignore_files=[".myignore", "config/search.ignore"])

docs.title: Symbolic links and file systems
docs.text:
• follow_symlinks=True makes the walker descend into directories reached through symbolic links. The default is False.
  • same_file_system=True stops the walker from crossing into other mounted file systems below the root. The default is False.

docs.title: Sorting
docs.text:
sort collects all results and sorts them before returning a list:

Value Order "name" File name only (the last path component) "path" Full path string "size" File size, smallest first "mtime" Modification time, oldest first

Any other value raises VexyGlobError. search() ignores sort.

docs.title: Threads
docs.text: threads sets the number of walker threads. None (the default) or 0 uses the number of logical CPUs.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: vexy-glob needs Python 3.8 or newer. The compiled part is a single extension module, vexy_glob._vexy_glob, built against the stable Python ABI (abi3), so one wheel per platform covers every supported Python version.

docs.title: Install from PyPI
docs.text:
1. Install the package with uv:

    uv pip install vexy-glob

    Or with pip:

    python -m pip install vexy-glob

  2. Check that the extension loads:

    python -c "import vexy_glob; print(vexy_glob.__version__)"

    The command prints the installed version.

  3. Check that the vg command is on your PATH:

    vg find "*.py" --depth 1

    The command lists Python files in the current directory.

The package depends on fire and rich, which the CLI uses. pip and uv install them automatically.

docs.title: Wheels and source builds
docs.text:
The release workflow builds wheels for these platforms:

Platform Architectures Linux (manylinux) x86_64, aarch64 macOS x86_64, arm64 Windows x64

If PyPI has no wheel for your platform, pip downloads the source distribution and compiles it. That needs a Rust toolchain:

  1. Install Rust from https://rustup.rs/.
  2. Run the install command again. pip calls maturin, which runs cargo build --release and packages the result. The first build downloads and compiles the Rust dependencies, which takes a few minutes.

docs.title: Install from a Git checkout
docs.text:
Prerequisites: Python 3.8 or newer, a Rust toolchain and uv.

  1. Clone the repository:

    git clone https://github.com/vexyart/vexy-glob.git
cd vexy-glob

  2. Create a virtual environment:

    uv venv --python 3.12
source .venv/bin/activate

  3. Build the extension and install it into the environment in editable mode:

    uv pip install maturin
maturin develop --release

    maturin develop compiles src/*.rs, places the extension next to vexy_glob/__init__.py and installs the package. Leave out --release for a faster, unoptimised debug build.

  4. Run the tests to confirm the build:

    uv pip install pytest
python -m pytest tests/ -q

docs.title: Build a wheel yourself
docs.text:
./build.sh package builds the source distribution and one wheel for the current machine into dist/, then runs twine check on both:

./build.sh package
ls dist/

vexy_glob-1.0.9-cp38-abi3-macosx_11_0_arm64.whl
vexy_glob-1.0.9.tar.gz

The version in the file names comes from the version field in Cargo.toml.

docs.title: Uninstall
docs.text: uv pip uninstall vexy-glob

docs.title: Patterns and case
docs.text: The pattern argument of find(), glob(), iglob() and search() is a glob pattern compiled by the Rust globset crate. This page explains which part of each path the pattern is compared with, and how letter case is handled.

docs.title: What the pattern is compared with
docs.text: The walker produces paths that start with the root you passed: ./src/a.py for the default root ".", src/a.py for root="src", /home/me/a.py for an absolute root. The pattern is tested against that whole string, but the tool first rewrites patterns that contain no path separator.

docs.title: Patterns without / match at any depth
docs.text:
If the pattern contains neither / nor \, the tool puts **/ in front of it. So *.py becomes **/*.py, which matches a .py file in any directory below the root.

Pattern you pass Pattern that is matched Matches ./src/sub/b.py? *.py **/*.py yes b.py literal file-name comparison yes src/*.py src/*.py no **/src/*.py **/src/*.py yes ./src/*.py ./src/*.py yes

This is the main difference from Python's glob.glob(), where *.py only looks in one directory. To limit the depth, use max_depth (see Filters).

docs.title: Patterns with / are matched against the full path
docs.text:
A pattern with a separator is used as is, so it has to describe the path from its first character. With the default root, paths start with ./:

>>> vexy_glob.find("src/*.py", as_list=True)
[]
>>> sorted(vexy_glob.find("./src/*.py", as_list=True))
['./src/a.py', './src/sub/b.py']

Two ways to avoid the ./ prefix problem:

  • Start the pattern with **/, for example **/src/*.py.
  • Pass the directory as root and keep the pattern short: find("*.py", root="src").

docs.title: * also matches /
docs.text: globset is used without its "literal separator" option, so * can match across directory separators. In the example above, ./src/*.py matched ./src/sub/b.py. Use max_depth or an exclude pattern when you need to stop at one level.

docs.title: Pattern syntax
docs.text:
Syntax Meaning Example * Any run of characters, including / *.md ? Any single character file?.txt ** Any number of directories **/tests/*.py [abc], [a-z] One character from a set or range img[0-9].png [!abc] One character not in the set [!_]*.py {a,b} Either alternative *.{py,pyi}

A pattern without any of * ? [ ] { } is a literal. Literals take a faster path:

  • A literal without / is compared with the file name only: README.md matches ./README.md and ./docs/README.md.
  • A literal with / matches any path that ends with it: sub/b.py matches ./src/sub/b.py.

docs.title: Smart case (the default)
docs.text:
case_sensitive defaults to None, which selects smart case:

  • The glob pattern is case-sensitive if it contains an uppercase letter, and case-insensitive otherwise.
  • The content regex (for search() or content=) follows the same rule on its own: a regex with an uppercase letter is case-sensitive.
>>> vexy_glob.find("readme.md", as_list=True)   # no uppercase: insensitive
['./README.md']
>>> vexy_glob.find("Readme.md", as_list=True)   # uppercase: sensitive
[]

docs.title: Forcing a mode
docs.text:
Pass case_sensitive=True or case_sensitive=False. The value then applies to both the glob pattern and the content regex:

>>> sorted(vexy_glob.find("*.PY", case_sensitive=False, as_list=True))
['./src/a.py', './src/sub/b.py']

exclude patterns use the same case mode as the main pattern.

docs.title: Invalid patterns
docs.text:
A pattern that globset cannot parse raises PatternError:

>>> vexy_glob.find("[", as_list=True)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
vexy_glob.PatternError: Invalid glob pattern: error parsing glob '**/[': unclosed character class; missing ']': '['

The message shows the rewritten pattern (**/[), which tells you that the **/ prefix was added.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text: This page walks through one small project so you can see what each call returns. You need vexy-glob installed (see Installation).

docs.title: Set up a sample tree
docs.text:
1. Create a scratch directory with a few files:

    mkdir -p play/src/sub play/.hid
cd play
echo "import os" > src/a.py
echo "TODO x" > src/sub/b.py
echo "hello" > README.md
echo "x" > .hid/c.py

  2. Start Python in play/:

    python

docs.title: Find files
docs.text:
1. Import the package and list the Python files:

    >>> import vexy_glob
>>> sorted(vexy_glob.find("*.py", as_list=True))
['./src/a.py', './src/sub/b.py']

    Three things happened:

    • *.py has no /, so the pattern matched file names at any depth.
    • Paths start with ./ because the default root is ".".
    • .hid/c.py is missing, because hidden files and directories are skipped by default.

  2. Include hidden entries:

    >>> sorted(vexy_glob.find("*.py", hidden=True, as_list=True))
['./.hid/c.py', './src/a.py', './src/sub/b.py']

  3. Search below a different root. The paths now start with that root:

    >>> sorted(vexy_glob.find("*.py", root="src", as_list=True))
['src/a.py', 'src/sub/b.py']

  4. Stream instead of collecting. Without as_list=True, find() returns an iterator that yields each path as the walker finds it:

    >>> it = vexy_glob.find("*.py")
>>> for path in it:
...     print(path)
./src/sub/b.py
./src/a.py

    The order depends on thread scheduling. Use sort="path" (which also collects the results into a list) when the order matters.

  5. Get pathlib.Path objects:

    >>> vexy_glob.find("README.md", as_path=True, as_list=True)
[PosixPath('README.md')]

    On Windows the objects are WindowsPath.

docs.title: Filter
docs.text:
1. Directories only:

    >>> vexy_glob.find("*", file_type="d", sort="path")
['.', './src', './src/sub']

    The root directory itself is part of the walk, so "." appears.

  2. Files by extension, sorted by file name:

    >>> vexy_glob.find("*", extension=["py", "md"], file_type="f", sort="name")
['./README.md', './src/a.py', './src/sub/b.py']

  3. Files changed in the last day:

    >>> sorted(vexy_glob.find("*.py", mtime_after="-1d", as_list=True))
['./src/a.py', './src/sub/b.py']

docs.title: Search contents
docs.text:
1. Search for a regular expression in Python files:

    >>> vexy_glob.search("TODO", "*.py", as_list=True)
[{'path': './src/sub/b.py', 'line_number': 1, 'line_text': 'TODO x\n', 'matches': ['TODO x']}]

    Each result is a dictionary. line_text keeps the line ending.

  2. Search with a lowercase pattern. Smart case makes it case-insensitive, so it still finds TODO:

    >>> [r["path"] for r in vexy_glob.search("todo", "*.py")]
['./src/sub/b.py']

docs.title: Use the command line
docs.text:
The same searches from a shell:

vg find "*.py"
vg search "*.py" "TODO" --no-color

./src/sub/b.py
./src/a.py
./src/sub/b.py:1:TODO x

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Patterns and case explains how patterns meet paths.
  • Filters lists every filter and its accepted values.
  • Python API is the full reference.

docs.title: A call with as_list=True never returns
docs.text:
Symptom. With vexy-glob 1.0.9 or earlier, find(..., as_list=True), find(..., sort=...), glob() or search(..., as_list=True) hangs on a large tree, while the same call without as_list finishes quickly.

Cause. In those releases the list path waited for the walker to finish before it read results from the internal channel. When the number of results exceeded the channel capacity, the walker blocked and the call waited forever. The capacity is 1,000 results by default, 500 matching lines for content search, 10,000 with sort, and 1,000 × threads (at most 8,000) when you pass threads. See Architecture.

Fix. Upgrade to vexy-glob 1.0.11 or later, where the list path drains the channel while the walker runs:

uv pip install --upgrade vexy-glob

Workaround for older releases. Use the iterator and build the list in Python:

paths = list(vexy_glob.find("**/*.txt"))           # instead of as_list=True
paths = sorted(vexy_glob.find("**/*.txt"))         # instead of sort="path"
hits = list(vexy_glob.search("TODO", "*.py"))      # instead of as_list=True
paths = list(vexy_glob.iglob("*.py"))              # instead of glob()

docs.title: ImportError: vexy_glob extension module not built
docs.text:
The Python files were imported without the compiled module vexy_glob/_vexy_glob.*. This happens when you run Python from the root of a source checkout, where the local vexy_glob/ directory shadows the installed package.

  • In a source checkout, build the extension: maturin develop.
  • Otherwise, run your script from another directory, or install the package (uv pip install vexy-glob).

docs.title: No results, or fewer than expected
docs.text:
Work through these causes in order:

  1. The pattern contains /. Such patterns must match the whole path, which starts with the root (./ by default). src/*.py matches nothing; use **/src/*.py, ./src/*.py or find("*.py", root="src"). See Patterns and case.
  2. Case. A pattern with an uppercase letter is case-sensitive: Readme.md does not match README.md. Pass case_sensitive=False.
  3. Hidden files. Names starting with a dot, and everything inside hidden directories, are skipped. Pass hidden=True.
  4. Ignore files. .gitignore, .ignore, .git/info/exclude, the global Git ignore file and a root .fdignore can hide entries. Pass ignore_git=True to switch off all but the global Git ignore file.
  5. Extension written with a dot. extension=".py" matches nothing; use extension="py".
  6. Depth. With max_depth, the root is level 0. A file in ./src/ is at level 2.
  7. Wrong root. A root that does not exist gives an empty result and, in iterator mode, a line on standard error: Error during traversal: nope: No such file or directory (os error 2).

docs.title: More results than expected
docs.text:
• A pattern without / matches at every depth: *.py is treated as **/*.py. Use max_depth to stay near the root.
  • * also matches /, so ./src/*.py includes files in ./src/sub/.
  • vexy_glob.glob("*.py") searches subdirectories too, unlike glob.glob("*.py").
  • Without file_type, directories and links are returned along with files. find("*") also returns the root itself (.).

docs.title: PatternError or VexyGlobError on a regex
docs.text:
• PatternError: Invalid glob pattern: ... means the glob (or an exclude entry) has a syntax error, often an unclosed [ or {.
  • VexyGlobError: Invalid content regex: ... means the content regex does not compile. The Rust regex engine has no look-around and no backreferences; rewrite the pattern without them, or filter line_text in Python with re.

docs.title: ValueError: Invalid time format
docs.text: A time argument is a string the parser does not recognise. Accepted strings are ISO dates (2025-01-01), ISO date-times (2025-01-01T12:00:00, optional Z) and relative values -<number><unit> with unit s, m, h or d. Weeks (-1w) are not supported; write -7d.

docs.title: vg: Error: 'int' object has no attribute 'strip'
docs.text: --min-size or --max-size received a bare number. Add a unit: --min-size 500b, --min-size 10k. See Command line.

docs.title: vg -h does not show help
docs.text: -h is the short form of --hidden. Use vg --help, vg find --help or vg search --help.

docs.title: matches contains the whole line
docs.text: In the current release, the matches list of a search result holds the trimmed line, not the individual regex matches. Run Python's re.finditer() on line_text to get the matched substrings. See Content search.

docs.title: Messages on standard error during iteration
docs.text: Lines such as Error during traversal: ...: Permission denied come from the walker. The walk continues past the entry that failed. To skip a directory you cannot read, add it to an ignore file or to exclude.

docs.title: Installing fails with a Rust or cargo error
docs.text: pip found no wheel for your platform and is building from source. Install a Rust toolchain from https://rustup.rs/ and run the install again. See Installation.
